title: Shewa and the reduced vowels

objectives.can: Tell a vocal shewa from a silent one and recognise the three composite shewas.

explanation.summary: Two dots one above the other under a consonant are a shewa. Sometimes the shewa is silent and sometimes it is a very short vowel, and three related signs, the composite shewas, are used under the throat letters. Knowing which is which is the first step to dividing a word into its syllables.

sections.heading: One sign, two jobs
body: The shewa is written with two dots, one above the other, under a consonant: בְ. It has two jobs. In some places it marks that the consonant has no vowel after it, so that the consonant closes the syllable before it. This is the silent shewa. In other places it stands for a very short vowel, a flicker of e before the next consonant. This is the vocal shewa. The sign is the same, and the reader decides from the place it stands.

A vocal shewa is very short. Modern Hebrew speakers usually say it as a short e, and sometimes drop it; in the Tiberian tradition it was a brief vowel whose exact quality is disputed. When you read aloud, a short e like the one in 'the' is a fair rule of thumb.

sections.heading: Vocal or silent: the school rules
body: The traditional rules, as many grammars teach them, are in the first table. They are a school scheme. Grammarians disagree about details, for example about how to treat a shewa after a long vowel that carries no stress, and about whether a vocal shewa forms a syllable of its own. The rules cover the great majority of words.

The shewa is silent when it follows a short vowel and so closes a syllable, and when it stands under the last letter of a word. It is vocal at the beginning of a word, after a long vowel, as the second of two shewas in the middle of a word, and under a consonant that is doubled by a dagesh (a doubling dot, lesson H0.2.3).

sections.heading: Two shewas together
body: Two shewas can stand side by side in the middle of a word. The first closes a syllable and is silent; the second begins the next syllable and is vocal. At the end of a word two shewas stand together only rarely; in that case both are silent. The word יִשְׁמְעוּ shows the pattern in the middle: the shin carries a silent shewa, and the mem a vocal one.

sections.heading: The composite shewas
body: The throat letters א ה ח ע (and sometimes ר) do not take a plain shewa easily. Under them a vocal shewa is usually written as one of three composite shewas, each made of a shewa and a short vowel sign. They are the hatef patah, the hatef segol and the hatef qamets, 'hatef' meaning 'hurried'. The second table shows them under alef.
Each is a very short vowel, with the quality of the short vowel in its name. The hatef patah is common, the hatef segol is less so, and the hatef qamets is rare. They are always vocal.

misunderstandings: A shewa is not always silent, and it is not always a vowel. Look at where it stands: after a short vowel it is silent, and at the start of a word it is vocal.
A word never begins with a silent shewa. The sign under the first letter of a word is always vocal.
The composite shewas are not full vowels. They are very short and they always count as vocal.
The rules are traditional rules of thumb, not laws of nature. Where the grammarians differ, the sound of the word is the same; only the label changes.

deeper.heading: Does a vocal shewa make a syllable?
body: Traditional grammars treat a consonant with a vocal shewa as the beginning of a syllable of its own, or of a half-syllable. Some modern descriptions treat it instead as a transition sound that belongs with the following syllable. Either way the reading is the same, which is why the school rules above are enough for reading the text.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Both words have a vocal shewa. The first begins with the vav, 'and', carrying a shewa at the start of the word: it is vocal, a flicker of e before the next syllable. In the second word the shewa stands under the yod after a long vowel, the qamets under the he, and it is vocal here too.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: In וַיִּקְרָא the shewa stands under the qof, after a short vowel (the hireq under the yod), and it closes that syllable: silent. In לָיְלָה, the shewa under the yod follows a long vowel, the qamets under the lamed, and is vocal. The same sign, two different jobs, decided by the vowel before it.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: If one man sin against another, God shall judge him; but if a man sin against the LORD, who shall entreat for him?' But they hearkened not unto the voice of their father, because the LORD would slay them.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: יֶחֱטָא has a hatef segol under the het: a very short e where a throat letter would not take a plain shewa. יִשְׁמְעוּ has two shewas in a row. The first, under the shin, follows the short hireq and is silent; the second, under the mem, begins the next syllable and is vocal.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And on the seventh day God finished His work which He had made; and He rested on the seventh day from all His work which He had made.

examples.analysis: הַשְּׁבִיעִי begins with the article. The shin carries the dot that doubles it, and a shewa. A shewa under a doubled letter is vocal, so the word is read approximately ha-shshe-vi-i. The article's own vowel is a patah.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife Naomi, and the name of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Beth-lehem in Judah. And they came into the field of Moab, and continued there.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: נָעֳמִי has a hatef qamets under the ayin, a very short o, in a name. מַחְלוֹן has a shewa under the het after a patah, a short vowel, so the shewa is silent and the syllable closes on the het: mach-lon.

reading.why: Four verses full of shewas: vocal ones at the start of words (וְהָאָרֶץ, מְרַחֶפֶת), silent ones after short vowels (וַיְהִי, וַיִּקְרָא), one under a final letter (וְחֹשֶׁךְ), and a composite shewa in אֱלֹהִים. Read slowly and say, for each shewa, whether it is vocal or silent.
